issues.note: Intransitive tennis smash exists; value is right, and no closed-list pattern shows it.
Crash-for-vehicles fact repeated in compare note and synonym discrimination; one fact, one field.
smash up is a real phrasal verb (smash the place up); slug is right.
Intransitive 'the vase smashed into pieces' is natural and matches the sense.
Real use, but mainly British sports journalism; minor gap for an American-primary dictionary.
Core idea's 'so that it breaks or is beaten' misfits hit-hard and record senses.
Passive realizes the transitive pattern and is noted; label defensible, small point only.
Phrasal verbs are separate entries; see_also already points to smash-up-phrv.
smash it is mainly British informal; region label means mainly used there.
Verb plus its noun object with a slot; acceptable verb + noun item.
Same duplicated crash fact as the compare note.
Closed pattern list has no plain intransitive pattern; transitivity value covers it.
'is beaten' misleads learners; hitting and record senses involve no breaking.

findings.F1: The fact that crash is the usual word for vehicles is stated in both the sense 2 compare note and synonym_discrimination.
findings.F2: The core idea ('hit with great force, so that it breaks or is beaten') is inaccurate for the hit-hard and record senses, and 'beaten' is ambiguous.
